newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya opposition protests in parliament, streets.
newsitem.headline: Kenya opposition protests in parliament, streets.

text.p: Kenyan politicians fought inside Kenya's parliament on Thursday and riot police clashed with students as the opposition staged protests in the capital to press demands for sweeping constitutional reforms.
Opposition members of parliament disrupted Finance Minister Musalia Mudavadi's budget speech before the punch-up with MPs of the ruling Kenya African National Union (KANU).
Police and the feared paramilitary General Service Unit (GSU) clashed with hundreds of students in and around the University of Nairobi close to the city centre, witnesses said.
"The police used teargas and made repeated baton charges while the students threw missiles at them," a witness said.
The trouble died down after nightfall.

President Daniel arap Moi, who was in parliament during the chaos, has agreed to ease a tough law restricting public assemblies but ruled out any more constitutional reforms until after general elections to be held this year.
Opposition leaders say they have wide public support and were pleased with their headline-grabbing show in parliament.
"Things are now beginning to happen and we shall meet next Tuesday to plot our next course of action," Raila Odinga, one of the opposition chiefs, told Reuters.
The contents of the keenly awaited 1997/98 budget were still unknown to the public on Thursday night because Mudavadi's speech was rendered inaudible by the stamping and shouting of opposition MPs.
They waved banners saying "No Reforms, No Budget" and state television stopped its live broadcast of the speech as Mudavadi made his 13th attempt to start.
"The minister read his speech but nobody heard him at all. We managed to disrupt him and so our campaign was very successful," Odinga said.
Mudavadi explained his cautious budget at a calm news conference later but he described his experience in parliament as traumatic and warned the opposition about its tactics.
"That type of action can be responsible for capital flight," he said.
He reduced corporate and income taxes and announced moves to spur savings and improve Kenya's creaking infrastructure.
He blamed drought for projected 1997 growth in gross domestic product (GDP) at 4.0 percent against 4.6 percent in 1996.
The government imposed tight security in central Nairobi to foil opposition plans for a banned protest rally at parliament.
From early morning hundreds of police and GSU men were deployed at strategic points in and around the capital.
Armed with wooden staves, shields and teargas canisters, they sealed off the parliament building.
"Today a demonstration would have been suicidal so the tactic was abandoned at the 11th hour," said Willy Mutunga of the National Convention Assembly, a pro-reform umbrella group.
The normally bustling city centre was semi-deserted.
Shops as well as some schools and offices were closed with people fearing a violent confrontation between the security forces and activists demanding political reforms.
City centre banks remained open and the shilling was stable. Business on the Nairobi Stock Exchange was sluggish.
Moi, 73 this year, looks certain to extend his 19-year rule for another five years, because of the existing electoral rules and the deep personal and ethnic splits within the opposition.
A Western diplomat said the government was set to announce a concession by extending the registration of voters nationwide by two weeks from the original deadline of June 22.
The National Electoral Commission said on Wednesday it had so far registered only 5.1 million voters, half the estimated electorate in the country of nearly 30 million.
Despite the ban on the opposition rally, hundreds of KANU supporters were allowed to gather in central Nairobi.
"We do not need a permit to march because we are on the side of KANU. We are working with the police and we are ready to disrupt the opposition march," KANU official Joseph Nyakunde said.
